title: Markup Is Not Margin: The Pricing Mix-Up Quietly Setting Your Prices Too Low
linkedin:
Add 50% to your cost and you get a 50% markup. You do not get a 50% margin.

That one mix-up is quietly costing owner-led businesses profit on every sale, every quote, every job, and it rarely looks like a problem on any single transaction.

Here is the maths. A $100 job with a 50% markup sells for $150. The $50 profit is 33.3% of that $150 price, not 50%, because markup is calculated against cost and margin is calculated against price. Different denominators, different numbers, every time.

Run it the other way and the size of the gap gets clearer. A genuine 40% margin needs roughly a 66.7% markup, not 40%. A business that sets a 40% margin target and applies a 40% markup instead is actually pricing for a margin closer to 28.6%, a gap of more than eleven percentage points on everything it sells.

Pricing rules like this are rarely reviewed as often as they are inherited. A markup set years ago by a founder or picked up from an industry rule of thumb keeps running quietly in the background long after anyone checks whether it still delivers the margin the business actually needs.

With grand final trade and spring bookings lifting quote and repricing volume this week, more transactions than usual are running through whatever rule currently sits in the price list. A good week to check which number is actually running yours.

A quick pricing check worth ten minutes this week, especially with grand final trade and spring bookings pushing more quotes and repriced stock through the books than usual.

Markup and margin are not the same number, even though they get used interchangeably in daily conversation. Markup is the percentage added on top of cost. Margin is the percentage of the final sale price that ends up as profit. Add 50 percent to a $100 cost and the price becomes $150, but the profit is only 33.3 percent of that price, not 50 percent. The two figures only match at zero, and the gap widens the higher the target percentage climbs.

Most pricing rules in owner-led businesses were set once, a while ago, and have not been rechecked since, which means this mix-up can sit quietly in a price list for years without a single transaction looking obviously wrong. A short check against ten of your most common products or jobs, comparing the margin you believe you are pricing for against the margin you are actually achieving, usually settles the question within an afternoon.
